The room in which the photograph is taken looks out through a large window onto a courtyard with an overhanging corrugated iron roof and a woven grass perimeter fence, seen as a backdrop in other object images. It is likely to be the American Mission station at Nasir.

A clay ox (1936.10.85) as made by Nuer children, complete with pendant horn ornaments, placed on a stool standing on a table with papers scattered on it. The room in which the photograph is taken looks out through a large window onto a courtyard with an overhanging corrugated iron roof and a woven grass perimeter fence, seen as a backdrop in other object images. It is likely to be the American Mission station at Nasir.

A horizon of savannah, with smoke rising from grass-firing. Evans-Pritchard took numerous photographs of vegetation to document changes in the cattle-keeping environment during his fieldwork. The firing of grass was done to promote new shoots for cattle to eat during the dry season.
In the foreground is thick vegetation, possibly a section of garden, with several byre (luak) and hut roofs of homesteads visible beyond.

A number of cattle making their way across a plain, with a light coloured ox with tasselled decoration on its upright left horn, its right horn trained backwards. Youth decorated their favourite oxen in this manner for aesthetically pleasing effects, and the identification between them and their ox was such that they took their initiated name and prestige from it. In contrast to his two earlier fieldwork visits when photographing cattle was viewed suspiciously by the Nuer, Evans-Pritchard took numerous record images of them during his later field trips.

A section of a thorntree, with Evans-Pritchard's canvas tent pitched just the other side, visible under the branches. This image seems to have been taken during treks across western Nuerland in 1936. Evans-Pritchard took many photographs of the natural environment to record changes in the pastoral Nilotic economy throughout the annual cycle.

A clay ox as made by Nuer children, complete with pendant horn ornaments, placed on a stool standing on a table with papers scattered on it. The room in which the photograph is taken looks out through a large window onto a courtyard with an overhanging corrugated iron roof and a woven grass perimeter fence, seen as a backdrop in other object images. It is likely to be the American Mission station at Nasir.

It is likely to be the American Mission station at Nasir.

Several large birds in an open area of ground, some just taking off. To the left can be seen the hut of a homestead. The location is noted as Pattai (?modern Fathai) on the road from Akobo, the route that Evans-Pritchard seems to have followed to western Nuerland in 1936 after completing a survey of the Luo in Kenya.

A head-and-shoulders portrait of a man wearing a body-cloth with feather hair decoration [poor focus], standing next to the Sobat River. Evans-Pritchard notes that this man could be an Anuak, but his initiation scars suggest that he is Nuer.
A head-and-shoulders profile portrait of a youth, standing next to the Sobat River [dark image].

A large giraffe trap consisting of a 'wheel' of spikes in which the animal's foot would become caught. It is being held aloft by a length of fibre from a stick in a courtyard with a woven grass fence surrounding it. In other images it is clear that this was a courtyard fence at a mission or government property, most likely at Nasir.
Two youths sitting near the entrance to Evans-Pritchard's tent (note tent pegs), one cutting cicatrices into the shoulder of the other with a razor blade, to create a dotted pattern.

A distant view of a cluster of huts comprising a cattle camp, seen across a wide expanse of treeless grass savannah in western Nuerland. Dry season camps in western Nuerland were often formed close to pools and other more permanent water sources, whereas in eastern Nuerland large rivers such as the Sobat and Nyanding were favoured.

A head-and-shoulders profile portrait of a man with hair ash-plastered into a forward facing 'horn', leaning against a colonial brick building at Pek. Hair was plastered in this way as part of the process of dying the hair a reddish tint. The image was taken by A. N. Tucker, who worked as Linguistic Expert of non-Arabic languages for the Sudan Government from 1929 to 1931. Evans-Pritchard met Tucker when the latter visited his fieldsite in 1930, after which time he gave him these prints.

A three-quarter length portrait of a youth wearing a body cloth and ash-plastered hair standing in front of a woven grass fence, porbably at a mission or government station. This maybe the American Mission building at Nasir.
Looking towards a camp in Western Nuerland, with numerous cattle tethered amongst small huts. The hut in the foreground has mud-plastered walls and a small thatched top twisted into a finial.

A slightly distant view of a herd of cattle comprising a cattle camp, set in a wide expanse of treeless grass savannah in western Nuerland. It is probable that this is a very early dry season camp without huts being made, which fits with Evans-Pritchard's 1936 fieldwork which straddled the end of the rains with the beginning of the dry season. This may relate to the early November camp from Nyueny village described by Evans-Pritchard in one of his articles.
In the foreground is thick vegetation, possibly a section of garden, with several byre (luak) and hut roofs of homesteads visible beyond.

A group of carriers with baggage resting near trees. Evans-Pritchard has evidently walked some distance away from them and turned back to take a photograph of the wooded country they were walking through.

A group of men standing in on a bank of mud and vegetation in the river, one carrying some harpoons and another resting against a long stick. These men may be clearing floating vegetation from the river (sudd) which exacerbates localized flooding, or constructing an area where fish may be driven and speared.

In the foreground is an ox with hump and large horns and par or rial markings (depending on the colour). Other cattle belonging to the homestead can be seen beyond, with the thatch of huts just visible to the right.

A group of youths in the foreground, with one resting his head on a wooden neckrest or headrest as another youth places his hand around his chin, plucking hairs from his chin. Younger boys sit next to them watching the camera. Beyond is a goat grazing in a sparsely wooded area. In another image it is clear that they are resting in the shade of Evans-Pritchard's tent.

A riek spirit-shrine post in the foreground set in the earth near a hut, with a reed fence beyond. Near it is a swept area with ?mat rolls placed around it and a pile of stones in the middle. This domestic ceremony place may have been made for a particular spirit that was causing illness and that needed sacrifice to appease it.

A young boy sits at the entrance way to a village hut, with large gourd containers nearby, along with an oil lamp and a tin bowl. The thatched entrance way is supported by a loosely arranged stake wall that allows light and air into a sort of extended frontal porch, with the entrance into the main hut just visible at the back.

A view across the cleared area of a village homestead (gol) with cattle lying down in the middle ground and a cattle byre (luak) to the left, a sleeping hut to the right and the cattle byre (luak) of another homestead beyond. In the central cleared area can just be seen a firescreen (buor) against which a cooking-fire is made. Often these firescreens incorporated three humps on the top, and were a symbol of a woman's status as a wife and mother of a household. Sacrifices were often made near to the buor of the homestead.

To the left can be seen windbreaks and cattle of a camp, probably near permanent water such as the Sobat River, with a cattle byre (luak) and sleeping huts with layered thatch behind. It is probable that this location is one of the Nuer Lou dry season camps on the Sobat River.
Looking towards the cleared ground of a homestead with a stake-walled cattle byre (luak) visible ahead and sleeping huts surrounding it, some with a distinctive extended entrance area.
A group of boys, one walking and two sitting, with spears nearby.
A group of boys, one walking and two sitting, with spears nearby.

Riek spirit-shrine posts set in the earth within a courtyard, with a reed fence beyond. A woman is sweeping the area around a pile of small stones placed near the shrine, where ceremonies were held, and a young girl watches her.

The canvas tent used by Evans-Pritchard during his Nuer fieldwork placed under a tree for shade. A chair sits in the doorway with boxes of various provisions stored under the tent-flaps. The location is probably at a village site, possibly in the Bahr-el-Ghazal region, and therefore possibly during Evans-Pritchard's first field trip in 1930.
